summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (no. 51) on 1 March 2023 and applied uniformly across all of Spain's autonomous communities. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may rectify the sex marker on their own civil registry entry by simple declaration before the Civil Registry, with no prior medical diagnosis of gender dysphoria and no requirement of two years of medical treatment; corresponding identity documents are adapted to the new marker, and the law's transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Self-identification replaced the former diagnostic and treatment pathway, placing Spain alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in using an administrative route to legal gender change. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16; the age-12 provision proved contentious in the Congress of Deputies.

The same statute bans medically unnecessary normalising surgeries on intersex children before consent, expands access to assisted reproduction, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, so the registry entry a visitor carries is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Beneath the national framework Canarias carries its own protections. Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 prohibits discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognises trans persons' rights, and the community has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities to do so before the national law of 28 February 2023. Canarias is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies.
tangentialFactors:
Access to sex-separated facilities on legal-gender lines contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban. A visitor moving between the two jurisdictions should expect different operative tests for the same facility.

Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations, which shapes the environment a trans visitor encounters in resort areas without altering the legal regime that applies elsewhere in the archipelago.

A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change. The finding is a dated baseline that predates the 2023 law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Canarias benefit from a regional anti-discrimination statute, Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014, that predates the national trans law by nearly nine years and prohibits discrimination on gender-identity grounds while recognising trans persons' rights. The community also operates a same-sex couple registry created in 2003.

Canarias is listed among the Spanish communities that ban conversion therapies, and it permitted self-declaration of legal gender from 2021, ahead of the national route opening in 2023.

For residents, the national statute's operative provisions include expanded access to assisted reproduction, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Legal gender change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation.

Minors aged 12 to 16 fall under the statute's consent rules for medical procedures, and recognition of gender identity is available from age 12 under conditions. Applications for rectification that were pending when the law entered into force are governed by its transitory provisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not name the instrument by which Canarias bans conversion therapies, so the statute or regulation carrying that ban is unresolved here.

No Canarias-specific enforcement of the gender-identity aggravating circumstance or of Article 510 is sourced. The two documented cases, Vigo in July 2026 and Valencia in January 2026, both sit outside this community, and whether the aggravation has been applied in a Canarias court is not established by the inventory.

Whether Canarias has issued autonomous implementing rules for Ley 4/2023 beyond Ley 8/2014, for example on facility access or on registry procedure, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The 2016 23-country survey predates the 2023 law and cannot be read as measuring opinion under the current regime.
